explanation: Mixed bag with a legal/formal-document lean: strongest on the colon after 'BY' in attorney signature blocks, and moderately on tokens in court captions, immigration/legal names, email header fields ('From:'), and some network/code identifiers (tcphdr, bind). No single token or context explains most examples.

Fires on a token that completes a very common fixed boilerplate phrase: the dash in '(Reuters) -', 'Press' in 'Associated Press', 'Policy' in 'Privacy Policy', 'to' in 'easy to'/'Welcome to', 'recent' in 'most recent', 'copyright', 'Duplicate'. Strength depends on how formulaic and predictable the phrase is; ordinary prose tokens are weak.

Fires on the second or later piece of a highly predictable multi-token fixed expression or name, e.g. '/android' in the Android XML namespace URL, 'assistance' in 'ineffective assistance', 'uts' in 'Tax Cuts', 'IZATION' in 'Naturalization', 'editor' in 'Letter to the editor', 'more' in 'one or more'. Ordinary unpredictable tokens are weak.

Fires on a verb (or the word right after a governing word) that follows an infinitive 'to'/purpose construction or a quantifier frame, e.g. 'to [present]', 'to [test]', 'to [improve]', 'to [refresh]', 'focus [all]', 'deler [av]'; also appears in non-English text (Norwegian, Albanian, Turkish, Finnish). Strongest on the main verb right after 'to' expressing a purpose.

Fires on words about fluids, gases and flow: water, oxygen, gas, respirable, pressure, drinking water, plus data 'stream'/'pipe' and HTTP headers ('Accept', 'Content-Type') in code. The common theme is something flowing through a channel (physical fluids/gases or data streams).

Fires on a word-initial token starting with 'U'/'u', especially 'Ul'/'Un'/'U' at the start of a capitalized word or name (Ulrik, Ultrasound, Ultron, Uppsala, UNABLE, UML, UWP). Lowercase 'ul'/'un' word starts fire moderately; 'under'/'user' weakly.

Fires on tokens inside US court opinions and legal procedural text: the space before a rule number ('Rule 73', 'P. 8.2'), and function words in stock judicial phrasing ('This matter is before the court', 'dispense with a hearing', 'pro se', 'Defendants and Appellants', 'for appellant'). Outside legal documents it is weak.

Fires on broken/partial UTF-8 byte tokens (shown as the replacement character) inside multi-byte characters, mainly in Hindi, Japanese, Chinese and emoji text. It is strongest at the start of a split character, often right after a space; ordinary ASCII tokens are near zero.

Fires on a verb or content word right after a modal/infinitive or a verb-of-intention frame where the meaning is about doing/forcing/creating something ('need to [force]', 'in order to [create]', 'not intended to [impose]', 'MUST AG[REE]', 'as if it [never]', 'I [want]'). This is a fuzzy syntactic-semantic pattern with many odd examples (math expressions too).

Fires on the token that finishes a highly predictable phrase or word in a variety of settings ('ineffective ass[istance]', 'claim [back]dated', 'not responsible [for]', 'How to [say]', 'cheated [on]', 'Dallas [Cowboys]', citation tags like 'sensors'). Similar to a general 'predictable continuation' detector; not tied to one topic.

Mostly fires in biomedical/scientific abstracts on tokens like 'SE' or '+/-' in 'mean +/- SE', and on nouns such as 'cases', 'outcome', 'experience', 'injury', but also on scattered tokens in code and general prose ('order', 'new', 'a'). The scientific-statistics part is the clearest; the rest is mixed.

Fires mainly on the '#' in Markdown/pandoc section anchors like 'Introduction {#sec1}' (around 83% very consistently), and also on separator tokens like ':' or '=' after a key in code/config. Other prose tokens fire only weakly.

Fires on the second word of a multi-word name or compound noun phrase where the first word strongly predicts it: 'Queen [Mary]', 'Saint [Mary]', 'San [Juan]', 'fridge [freezer]', 'parking lot', 'Medical [Research]', 'young [adults]', and code identifiers like 'horizontal_margin', 'num_faces'.

Fires on the head noun of a compound term or label used as a field/document-structure item, e.g. 'REFERENCE POINTS', 'Tax Return', 'Intelligence Tasks', 'executionOrder', 'composite design', 'Media caption', 'television schedule', 'NOTICES'. Strength rises when the word forms a fixed technical or administrative term.

Fires on a scattered mix: indentation/'import' tokens at the start of lines in Java/Android XML code, commas/spaces in copyright year lists, timestamp digits, and assorted words in foreign-language prose ('que', 'hid'). There is a weak 'structural token in code/boilerplate' theme but many examples don't fit.

Fires on code tokens at the start of a declaration or statement, especially return types after 'public' ('int', 'void'), 'import', 'def', 'function', 'super', and the object variable before a method call ('e.printStackTrace'). Fires only in program source code.

Fires on a token beginning with the letter 'P'/'p' at the start of a word, especially a capitalized name or word ('P'ichia, 'P'aphos, 'P'urification, 'P'uzzle, iPads, Luis Pardo). Lowercase/mid-word 'p' fires more weakly.

Fires on citation and cross-reference markup in academic text: the '@' in '[@b9]' reference tags, '#' in '{#sec1}' anchors, 'ref-type', 'CR' in '[@CR2]'. Weaker on '$' and spaces before numbers in patents/prose.

Fires on a word-continuation or name-completion token in a wide range of contexts: '.' in 'So.2d' case citations, 'Corporation' in 'NVIDIA Corporation', mid-word pieces of names and identifiers ('oto' in Botox, 'ande', 'age', 'kun'), and words like 'evaluate', 'chance', 'rules'. No clear unifying theme.

Fires on an assortment of tokens: pieces of foreign names (Shkodran, Sayyar, McLaughlin), function words in French/Portuguese text, digits inside version or gene numbers, and 'On' at a sentence start in legal text. No coherent single pattern.
